images.caption: The second building associated with hotelier and Klondike gold rush veteran Louis Anderson, it was built in 1902 at 5140 (originally 196) Ballard Ave NW for use as a lodging house and saloon operated by Charles Berryman. James Stephens of Seattle was the architect.

images.caption:
Plaque on the building, giving an inaccurate date of construction
The Anderson Building at 5201 (originally 201-3) Ballard Ave NW was built in 1900, the first of several built by hotel and saloon owner Louis Anderson after his successful return from the gold fields in Alaska. The second story was used for lodgings, known as the Hazelton House. In 1928 Clinton McClure, then the landlord of the Hazelton, was arrested after attempting to burn the building to the ground by inserting numerous jars of gasoline in the ceiling connected to a gas stove with a tube, endangering the lives of the hotel's 20 residents. There were no injuries and damages were only $500. This building can be seen in the film "Harry and The Hendersons" as the location of the hunting shop. It is currently undergoing restoration to return its windows to a more historic configuration.

images.caption: This building at 5219-21 Ballard Ave NW was constructed in 1902 by Seattle businessman John A. Landstrom. In the 1910s the upper floor was occupied by the local chapter of the infamous w:Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) and later served as a hotel under names such as The Annex and the St. Elmo. By the mid 1950s, the building was heavily deteriorated and close to condemnation, in May 1962, the building was completely remodeled to the pictured appearance and its neighbor demolished to shore up the walls.  For over 40 years it was occupied by a paint supply store, whose signage remained on the building even after it became the home of Bop Street Records, which would move to a new location in the 2010s before closing for good in 2020. The Landstrom Building was miraculously restored to its original condition in 2016.

images.caption: This building was built about 1905 by John Bevery and like many in the neighborhood contained lodging rooms on the upper floors. John Bevery and his family, most of whom worked at the Stimson Mill, lived in the building. It has since been restored from its dilapidated state in this photo.

images.caption: One of many triangular buildings formed by Ballard's unique street grid, the Bourgett Block was built in 1902 by James Bourgett after his previous building burned down. Initially housing Bourgett's saloon on the ground floor and offices above, it was later occupied by the first location of Ballard's Bartell drug store. The building is Romanesque in design, trimmed with Tenino sandstone. The architect was T.N. Larsen. The corner once featured a circular bay window with a conical roof, which was removed sometime in the 1930s. Uncontrolled vines on the facade have led to the loss of most of the building's cornice.

images.caption: The Bowie Building, located at 5348 Ballard Avenue NW, was originally built in 1895 by Norwegian immigrant and eventual Ballard mayor (1 term in 1901) John Johnson for his grocery store and residence in the Victorian style with protruding bay windows. Johnson was gone by 1908 and the ground floor was divided into two stores, with the northern half (5350) housing a grocery store then a hardware store for most of the 1930s. The southern storefront (5348) initially housed an unsuccessful theater then a succession of short-lived automobile related businesses until 1920 when it became the battery & electric shop of A.M. Arntzen and later the Sterling Electric Company. The building's current name comes from the longest lasting business at the address, Bowie Electric Co., started by Mitchell T. Bowie in 1916. Bowie bought out Sterling (and the building itself) in 1921 and not long after had the current façade constructed. He lived in the building's second floor apartment and by the late 1930s his store occupied the entire ground floor, sharing the space with Seattle City Light's branch office. The business lasted here well into the 1980s.

images.caption: The Chopard Block was constructed from 1893 to 1894 by Seattle saloonkeeper Louis S. Chopard and was originally 2-stories tall, with it and the neighboring Theisen Block both losing their upper floors in the 1960s. Chopard moved his living quarters into the building upon completion, which also had rooms for rent as the Chopard House. It was renamed the Tyson block about 1906 and later became a corner building when Ione Place was extended south to connect to Ballard Ave.

images.caption: The Cors & Wegener Block at the corner of Ballard Ave NW & 20th Ave, is one of Ballard's most historic and attractive 19th century buildings. It was constructed in 1893 by William Cors and R.E. Wegener to house lodging rooms and their saloon, which quickly gained a reputation as one of the roughest in town. The Ballard post office was relocated to the room next to the saloon in 1894, causing a public outcry; it would remain there until 1898. Ballard's main newspaper, the Ballard News was published in the building's upstairs in the 1900s.

images.caption: This massive triangular building at the corner of Leary Ave NW & 20th Ave NW was constructed in 1911 for the William M. Curtiss Hardware Company. Curtiss, one of the pioneer businessmen of Ballard, opened a tin shop on this site in 1889. The following year he built a 2-story addition and put in a stock of hardware. He soon became the leading hardware dealer in the city. He commissioned popular Seattle architect Victor W. Voorhees to design this building, which was originally envisioned to reach 5-stories tall. Curtiss passed away in 1927 and his company, in an ambitious move to expand, opened a branch store on Second Avenue in downtown Seattle in 1930 but were soon hit hard by the Great Depression, and were bankrupt by 1932. Their Ballard building was divided into apartments and the ground floor became a furniture store. It once featured large plate glass display windows on the lower floors before the building was converted entirely into apartments, sometime in the 1960s.

images.caption: This modest building at 5205 Ballard Ave NW was  built in 1915, one of many such filler buildings built after Ballard's boom. Shortly after its construction it housed a barber shop and in the 1920s was home to the U.S. Army Goods store. It contained a hamburger stand in the 1930s and was later an upholstery shop.

images.caption: The Hansen Building at Ballard Avenue and Park Place was built in 1905. Its first tenants were the Henry Brothers, Harry and Charles, who ran a saloon and hotel in the building, as well as calling it home. The saloon was later known as the North Star Bar, the ghost ad of which can still be seen on the building's north wall. During prohibition the ground floor became Ballard Laundry which it remained for several decades. It is currently a Filson store on the ground floor with offices above.

images.caption: This concrete building at 4763 (sometimes 4765) Ballard Ave was built about 1914 to house Ballard's first Ford dealership, Fairchild, Higgins & Matthews. Fairchild left the partnership in 1917 and in 1919 the firm relocated to a new building on Nickerson Street at the south end of the Fremont Bridge, leaving Ballard without a Ford dealer for several years. After Higgins & Matthews' moved out, the W.S. Dulmage Motor Co., a Chevrolet dealer based on Pike Street in Capitol Hill, opened their Ballard branch here. Less than a year later they were replaced by the branch of another Capitol Hill Chevrolet dealer, the Whitley Motor Co. but their stay would too be brief before a new Ford dealership, Wilson & Kreitle Inc. was established and moved into the building in 1921. In 1923 they relocated to a new larger building at 5320 Ballard Ave where, later known just as Wilson Ford Co., would remain for decades. Since the mid-1930s this building has been occupied by the Ballard Sheet Metal Works, which has been in business on this block since 1907.
